extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, registered patent practitioners, and USPTO examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing, evaluating, and deciding petitions to revive abandoned U.S. patent applications (37 CFR 1.137), including what constitutes acceptable replies, fee and timing requirements, and the standards/evidence for unintentional vs. unavoidable delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue fee payment as condition of revival
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 151 and 35 U.S.C. 41(a)(7) require payment of the issue fee as a condition to revive an application abandoned or a patent lapsed for failure to pay the issue fee; filing a continuing application without payment of the issue fee (or any outstanding balance) is not an acceptable reply to such an abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the issue fee increases between Notice of Allowance and payment, the Office will mail a notice requiring payment of the balance. The phrase 'for failure to pay the issue fee or any portion thereof' applies to failure to pay either the fee required in the Notice of Allowance or the balance required in a subsequent notice. The reply to revive must include the full issue fee then in effect or any outstanding balance, depending on whether a portion was previously submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication fee payment when abandoned for failure to pay publication fee
rubrics_metrics.description: An application abandoned for failure to pay the publication fee must include payment of the publication fee as the required reply to revive the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if revival is sought solely to maintain continuity with a continuing application, the petition to revive under 37 CFR 1.137 must include payment of the publication fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable replies for abandonment to a non-final action
rubrics_metrics.description: For a nonprovisional application abandoned for failure to reply to a non-final action, the required reply may be: (A) an argument or amendment under 37 CFR 1.111; or (B) the filing of a continuing application under 37 CFR 1.53(b) (or a CPA under 37 CFR 1.53(d) for design applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant of a petition under 37 CFR 1.137 is not a determination that the reply is complete. If the proposed reply to a non-final action appears bona fide, the petition may be granted; later, the examiner may find the reply lacking and issue a letter giving a 1-month shortened statutory period under 37 CFR 1.135(c) for correction (extensions under 1.136(a) permitted). If not corrected, application is again abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable replies for abandonment to a final action
rubrics_metrics.description: For abandonment for failure to reply to a final Office action, the reply required for consideration of revival must be one of: (A) a Notice of Appeal and appeal fee; (B) an amendment under 37 CFR 1.116 that cancels all rejected claims or otherwise places the application in condition for allowance; (C) filing an RCE under 37 CFR 1.114 accompanied by a submission meeting 37 CFR 1.111 and the requisite fee; or (D) filing a continuing application under 37 CFR 1.53(b) (or CPA under 1.53(d) for design applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a proposed amendment under 1.116 is filed as the reply, the Office of Petitions normally routes the application to the Technology Center to determine whether it places the application in condition for allowance. If the amendment does not place the application in condition for allowance, the examiner completes PTOL-303 and returns it to Office of Petitions (petition will not be granted). If the reply places the application in condition for allowance, the examiner should mark 'OK to enter upon revival.' Time for filing appeal brief will be set by Director if notice of appeal is used as reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reply required when abandonment is for failure to file an appeal brief
rubrics_metrics.description: When abandonment occurred due to failure to file an appeal brief, the reply required under 37 CFR 1.137(a)(1) or 1.137(b)(1) must be an appeal brief in compliance with 37 CFR 41.37(c) accompanied by the appeal brief fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As with other replies, after revival the examiner may determine the reply is lacking and issue a 1-month shortened statutory period under 1.135(c) to correct; extensions under 1.136(a) are permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office may require an RCE or continuing application where replies impose inordinate burden
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office may require filing of a continuing application or an RCE to meet the reply requirement of 37 CFR 1.137(a)(1)/(b)(1) where treating a reply under 37 CFR 1.111 or 1.113 would place an inordinate burden on the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplary circumstances: (A) the application has been abandoned for an inordinate period of time; (B) the application file contains multiple or conflicting replies to the last Office action; or (C) the reply or replies submitted under 1.137(a)(1)/(b)(1) are questionable as to compliance with 1.111 or 1.113.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements when filing an RCE as the reply
rubrics_metrics.description: When an RCE is filed as the reply to revive an application abandoned for failure to reply to a final Office action or failure to file an appeal brief, the submission accompanying the RCE must be a reply responsive within the meaning of 37 CFR 1.111 to the last Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consideration of responsiveness is done without factoring in the 'final' status of the action. The submission may be a previously filed amendment after final or a statement incorporating by reference arguments in a previously filed appeal or reply brief. The petition may be granted if the submission appears to be a bona fide attempt to provide a complete reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonpublication rescission and timely foreign filing notice requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant who made a nonpublication request but thereafter files a foreign counterpart that requires eighteen-month publication must rescind the nonpublication request and notify the Office of the foreign filing within forty-five days; failure to timely provide such notice results in abandonment under 35 U.S.C. 122(b)(2)(B)(iii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revival of such an abandonment is available only on the basis of 'unintentional' delay pursuant to 37 CFR 1.137(b) (not 'unavoidable' under 1.137(a)). The reply requirement of 1.137(c) is met by the notification of the foreign filing. Applicants may use form PTO/SB/64a to file a petition under 1.137(b). Filing a petition under 1.137(b) does not stay any period for reply that may be running against the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition fee requirement and nonrefundability
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for revival on the basis of unintentionally abandoned application or unintentionally delayed issue fee must be accompanied by the petition fee in 37 CFR 1.17(m), unless filed under 35 U.S.C. 133 or 151 (unavoidable delay), in which case fee is per 1.17(l). The petition fee is a statutory prerequisite and cannot be waived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase 'on filing' means the fee is required on filing (not merely at grant). The Office will not refund petition fees required by 1.17(l) or 1.17(m) regardless of dismissal/denial, and will not reach merits of petitions lacking the requisite fee. 'Unavoidable' delay petitions filed under 133 or 151 are a subset of petitions on the basis of unintentional delay; to obtain the lower fee under 1.17(l) the petition must be accompanied by an adequate showing that the entire delay was unavoidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unintentional delay standard and reliance on applicant statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions under 37 CFR 1.137(b) are evaluated under the 'unintentional delay' standard and are generally less burdensome; the Office typically accepts the applicant's statement that 'the entire delay ... was unintentional' without requiring further information in the vast majority of cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office relies on the applicant's duty of candor and good faith (37 CFR 10.18). If the Office requests further information, it usually requires only statements and perhaps copies of correspondence relevant to the period of delay. Making an inappropriate statement in a petition may have adverse enforcement consequences (e.g., inequitable conduct leading to unenforceability)—see cited case law (Lumenyte).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unavoidable delay standard and evidence required
rubrics_metrics.description: A showing of 'unavoidable' delay (37 CFR 1.137(a)) requires evidence beyond a statement: (1) evidence concerning procedures in place that should have avoided the error; (2) evidence of training and experience of persons responsible; and (3) copies of applicable docketing records showing the error caused the delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions under 1.137(a) must establish the delay was unavoidable (not merely unintentional). Because the 1.137(a) requirements are more exacting, such petitions are less likely to be grantable as filed and often require multiple interlocutory decisions requesting additional evidence until a satisfactory showing is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional or deliberate abandonment precludes unintentional/unavoidable finding
rubrics_metrics.description: An abandonment that resulted from an applicant's deliberately chosen course of action (e.g., deciding claims are unpatentable, not cost-justified, or intentionally deferring fees) is not 'unintentional' under 1.137(b) nor 'unavoidable' under 1.137(a). A change of mind after deliberate abandonment does not render the prior delay unintentional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed: (A) applicant considers claims unpatentable; (B) allowed/patentable claims not of sufficient breadth; (C) patent not worth expense; (D) not worth maintaining interest; (E) applicant seeks to defer fees and prosecution costs. Case law (In re Application of G; In re Maldague) supports this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended petition content for unintentional delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants filing a petition under 37 CFR 1.137(b) are advised to include the statement: 'the entire delay in filing the required reply from the due date for the reply until the filing of a grantable petition pursuant to 37 CFR 1.137(b) was unintentional,' and may include facts concerning the delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms provided by the Office (PTO/SB/64, PTO/SB/64a, PTO/SB/64PCT) may be used. Even if Office requires further information, a 1.137(b) petition remains significantly less burdensome than a 1.137(a) petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonably prudent person standard for unavoidable delay
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Unavoidable' delay is judged by the reasonably prudent person standard: requiring no more care than generally used by prudent persons in important business, permitting reliance on ordinary agencies (mail, telegraph), trustworthy employees and usual instrumentalities; unexpected failures of these agencies may be unavoidable if due care is otherwise shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions are made case-by-case taking all facts into account (Smith v. Mossinghoff). The petitioner bears the burden of establishing the delay was unavoidable; failure to meet the burden requires denial (Haines v. Quigg).

rubrics_metrics.name: Docketing/clerical error may justify unavoidable delay if criteria met
rubrics_metrics.description: A delay resulting from a clerical/docketing error by an employee may constitute 'unavoidable' delay if: (A) the error caused the delay; (B) a business routine existed for performing the clerical function that could reasonably be relied upon to avoid errors; and (C) the employee was sufficiently trained and experienced with regard to the function and routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited decisions: In re Egbers; In re Katrapat. Example: change of correspondence address leading to Office action mailed to old address—adequate showing requires evidence that due care was taken to notify change of address properly (see MPEP § 601.03) and that the notification was reasonably calculated to call attention to the change. The MPEP lists what does NOT constitute proper notification of address change.

rubrics_metrics.name: What does not constitute proper notification of change of correspondence address
rubrics_metrics.description: The following do not constitute proper notification of a change in correspondence address: (A) mere inclusion of a different address in a paper filed for another purpose without mention that address change is being made; (B) notification on a paper listing plural applications as affected (except as provided by Customer Number practice); (C) lack of notification or belated notification to the USPTO of the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For an abandonment caused by address change, an adequate showing of unavoidable delay must establish due care was taken to adhere to prompt notification requirements and include evidence that timely notification was filed in a manner reasonably calculated to call attention to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of knowledge or misapplication of rules/statute is not unavoidable delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay caused by lack of knowledge or improper application of the patent statute, rules of practice, or the MPEP does not constitute 'unavoidable' delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited: Haines v. Quigg; Vincent v. Mossinghoff; Smith v. Diamond; Potter v. Dann; Ex parte Murray. Examples: permitting maximum extendable statutory period to expire while awaiting a notice of allowance, failure to file papers/fees in compliance with 37 CFR 1.8 or 1.10, reliance on oral advice from USPTO employees, or USPTO's failure to advise do not make delay unavoidable (see In re Sivertz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three periods evaluated for delay and recommended filing windows
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of petitions considers three delay periods: (A) the delay in reply that caused abandonment; (B) delay in filing an initial petition under 37 CFR 1.137 to revive; and (C) delay in filing a grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.137.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office generally will not question whether delay was intentional/unavoidable if petition is filed: (1) within 3 months of the date applicant was first notified that the application was abandoned; and (2) within 1 year of the date of abandonment. If petition not filed within 3 months, Office may require showings as to how the delay was unavoidable (for 1.137(a)) or unintentional (for 1.137(b)). If 1.137(a) petition not filed within 1 year of abandonment, Office will require information when applicant first became aware and a showing how delay occurred despite due care. For 1.137(b) not filed within 1 year, Office may require further information as to when applicant became aware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion or refiling under different standard after denial
rubrics_metrics.description: Dismissal or denial of a petition under 37 CFR 1.137(a) does not preclude obtaining relief under 37 CFR 1.137(b) for unintentional delay (unless decision indicates otherwise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant may file a 1.137(b) petition accompanied by the fee in 1.17(m), required reply, an unintentionality statement, and any required terminal disclaimer. Forms PTO/SB/61 or PTO/SB/61PCT may be used to file a petition for revival of an unavoidably abandoned application (i.e., for unavoidable delay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and continued diligence until petition granted
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of establishing that the delay was unavoidable (for 1.137(a)) or unintentional (for 1.137(b)) remains with the applicant, including continuing to progress toward a grantable petition promptly until notified that the petition is granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. 133 and 151 require showing that delay was 'unavoidable' through the filing of a grantable petition without delay; failing to file promptly after becoming aware of abandonment undermines claims of unavoidable delay (In re Application of Takao; Application of S). The Office may treat delay in filing initial/ grantable petition as part of the overall delay to be assessed.
